meta.title: Who really said "Great works are performed not by strength but by perseverance"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Samuel Johnson wrote it, in Rasselas (1759), Ch. XIII, spoken by Imlac. The first edition reads “not by strength, but perseverance.”
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Great works are performed not by strength but by perseverance'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Samuel Johnson — from Rasselas (1759), spoken by the poet Imlac. The original wording omits the second “by.”

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: From Johnson’s prose tale The History of Rasselas, Prince of Abissinia (1759), Chapter XIII, where it is spoken by the poet Imlac to encourage the Prince as they tunnel through a mountain to escape. The first-edition text reads “not by strength, but perseverance”; the widely shared form adds a second “by.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The History of Rasselas, Prince of Abissinia

source.excerpt: “Sir,” said his companion, “practice will enable us to continue our labour for a longer time. Mark, however, how far we have advanced, and ye will find that our toil will some time have an end. Great works are performed not by strength, but perseverance; yonder palace was raised by single stones, yet you see its height and spaciousness. He that shall walk with vigour three hours a day, will pass in seven years a space equal to the circumference of the globe.”
trail: The exact sentence appears in the primary text: “Great works are performed not by strength, but perseverance” — Rasselas, Ch. XIII, Project Gutenberg.
The reputable Samuel Johnson Sound Bite Page attributes the line to Imlac in Rasselas and renders it “not by strength, but by perseverance.”
Johnson returned to the theme elsewhere: Wikiquote sources a companion passage on “the resistless force of perseverance” to The Rambler No. 43 (1750).
source.excerptNote: Imlac reassures the Prince during their exhausting attempt to hew an escape passage through the mountain that walls their valley.

author.name: Samuel Johnson
author.heading: About Samuel Johnson
author.bio: Samuel Johnson was one of the most quoted figures in English letters — essayist, moralist, poet, and compiler of the landmark Dictionary of the English Language (1755). His prose tale Rasselas (1759), reportedly written quickly to pay for his mother’s funeral, is a meditation on the pursuit of happiness. His balanced, aphoristic sentences made him a magnet for both genuine maxims and later loose paraphrase.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This one is genuinely Johnson’s — but two honest caveats travel with it.

items.why: The viral form “not by strength but by perseverance” smooths the first-edition text, which reads “not by strength, but perseverance” — see Rasselas, Ch. XIII. Reputable editions vary, so the added “by” is a normalization, not a fabrication.

items.who: Samuel Johnson vs. the character Imlac
items.why: The line is voiced by the fictional poet Imlac inside the tale, not asserted by Johnson in his own person — a caution the Samuel Johnson Sound Bite Page flags for all Rasselas quotations, though the sentiment is thoroughly Johnsonian.

misattribution.truthLine: Both the idea and the near-exact words are Johnson’s, from Rasselas (1759), Chapter XIII — the only liberty the internet takes is an extra “by.”

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: In Rasselas, the Prince of Abissinia is confined to a paradisal but imprisoning “happy valley.” Weary from trying to hew an escape passage through solid rock, he is tempted to give up. His companion Imlac answers with the maxim: monumental achievement comes not from a single burst of power but from steady, accumulated effort — the palace “raised by single stones.”

Johnson pressed the same conviction elsewhere, writing in The Rambler that the works “at which we look with praise or wonder, are instances of the resistless force of perseverance.” The Rasselas line simply gives that belief its most portable, motivational shape.
context.pull: “Yonder palace was raised by single stones, yet you see its height and spaciousness.”
